Local asymptotics and optimal control for a viscous Cahn-Hilliard-Reaction-Diffusion model for tumor growth

Elisa Davoli Address: Institute for Analysis and Scientific Computing, Vienna University of Technology, Wiedner Hauptstrasse 8-10, 1040 Vienna, Austria Email address: elisa.davoli@tuwien.ac.at , Elisabetta Rocca Address: Dipartimento di Matematica, Università di Pavia and IMATI - C.N.R., Via Ferrata 5, 27100 Pavia, Italy Email address: elisabetta.rocca@unipv.it , Luca Scarpa Address: Department of Mathematics, Politecnico di Milano, Via E. Bonardi 9, 20133 Milano, Italy Email address: luca.scarpa@polimi.it and Lara Trussardi Address: Institute of Mathematics and Scientific Computing, University of Graz, Heinrichstraße 36, 8010 Graz (Austria) Email address: lara.trussardi@uni-graz.at
Abstract.

In this paper we study nonlocal-to-local asymptotics for a tumor-growth model coupling a viscous Cahn-Hilliard equation describing the tumor proportion with a reaction-diffusion equation for the nutrient phase parameter. First, we prove that solutions to the nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard system converge, as the nonlocality parameter tends to zero, to solutions to its local counterpart. Second, we provide first-order optimality conditions for an optimal control problem on the local model, accounting also for chemotaxis, and both for regular or singular potentials, without any additional regularity assumptions on the solution operator. The proof is based on an approximation of the local control problem by means of suitable nonlocal ones, and on proving nonlocal-to-local convergence both for the corresponding dual systems and for the associated first-order optimality conditions.

Key words and phrases: 
Viscous nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard equation, reaction-diffusion equation, well-posedness, nonlocal-to-local convergence, optimal control, tumor growth models

1. Introduction

We study here diffuse interface tumor-growth models characterized by viscous nonlocal and local Cahn-Hilliard systems coupled with reaction-diffusion equations. This formulation was introduced first in [34] and successively studied in many papers in the literature both from the well-posedness [10, 11, 12, 23] and the optimal control [13, 15, 16] point of view.

Nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard type systems are currently the subject of an intense research activity. Among the vast literature we single out the contributions [1, 5, 26, 28, 33] and the references therein. The first proof of existence of solutions for nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard equations with singular kernels with lower than W1,1W^{1,1}-regularity was carried out by some authors of this paper in [17, 19], where nonlocal-to-local convergence of the associated solutions was also established both in the Dirichlet and in the viscous homogeneous Neumann setting. The case of W1,1W^{1,1} kernels was the subject of [18]. In the same work, the authors provided also a connection with the seminal works of Sandier and Serfaty in [39] on the evolutionary convergence of gradient flows with applications to Ginzburg-Landau functionals (see also [36, 39], as well as the study of a simplified tumor growth model in [38]). Nonlocal-to-local convergence results have then been obtained in more general settings such as coupled systems [3] and degenerate mobilities [7, 20]. Precise rates of convergence have been provided in [2]. The strict separation property was analyzed in [27, 37], whereas the case of degenerate mobility was the subject of [22].

In the present contribution we focus instead on nonlocal-to-local asymptotics for Cahn-Hilliard tumor-growth models. To the Authors’ knowledge, this is the first paper in the literature in this direction. In order to describe our results in details, we need to introduce some notation.

We denote by φ∈(−1,1)\varphi\in(-1,1) the difference in volume fractions between the tumor cells (φ=1\varphi=1) and the healthy cells (φ=−1\varphi=-1), and by σ∈(0,1)\sigma\in(0,1) the concentration of the nutrient. We then consider the following local problem in (0,T)×Ω(0,T)\times\Omega, where T>0T>0 is a fixed final time and Ω\Omega is a domain in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}:

∂tφ−div(m(φ)∇μ)=R−h(φ)u,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi-\operatorname{div}(m(\varphi)\nabla\mu)=R-h(\varphi)u\,, (1.1)
R=P⁡(φ)​(σ+χ⁡(1−φ)−μ),\displaystyle R=P(\varphi)(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi)-\mu)\,, (1.2)
μ=τ​∂tφ−Δ​φ+ψ′​(φ)−χ​σ,\displaystyle\mu=\tau\partial_{t}\varphi-\Delta\varphi+\psi^{\prime}(\varphi)-\chi\sigma\,, (1.3)
∂tσ−div[n(φ)∇(σ+χ(1−φ))]=−R+w.\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma-\operatorname{div}[n(\varphi)\nabla(\sigma+\chi(1-\varphi))]=-R+w\,. (1.4)

Here mm and nn are the (bounded from below and above) mobilities, τ>0\tau>0 is the viscosity coefficient, and χ≥0\chi\geq 0 is the chemotaxis coefficient. The potential ψ\psi is generally a double-well potential having two global minima in correspondence of the pure phases: in particular, the case of polynomial potentials of the form

ψ⁡(s)=14​(1−s2)2,s∈ℝ,\displaystyle\psi(s)=\frac{1}{4}(1-s^{2})^{2},\quad s\in\mathbb{R}, (1.5)

can be included in our analysis. The term RR on the right-hand side of the Cahn-Hilliard equation is motivated from linear phenomenological laws for chemical reactions (see [34]), and takes into account the proliferation and death of tumoral cells. As mentioned in [34], by means of proper numerical simulations, it is possible to show that the predominant term in (1.2) is the first one P⁡(φ)​σP(\varphi)\sigma, while the remaining terms are relevant only for large values of χ\chi. Moreover, the choice of RR automatically guarantees the thermodynamical consistency of the models, that is, the fact that the energy decreases along solutions in the case in which no source terms are present. The proliferation function PP calibrates the strength of the reaction terms and is usually taken as follows:

P⁡(s)={P0if ​s≤−1,P1−P02​(s+1)+P0if −1<s<1,P1if ​s≥1,P(s)=\begin{cases}P_{0}&\text{if }s\leq-1,\\ \frac{P_{1}-P_{0}}{2}(s+1)+P_{0}&\text{if }-1<s<1,\\ P_{1}&\text{if }s\geq 1,\end{cases} (1.6)

where P0P_{0} and P1P_{1} are suitable positive constants, so that the proliferation is faster in the tumor phase. There are possible different choices in the literature for the term RR on the right hand side, cf., e.g., [29, 30, 31, 40] and the references therein. Note that, for technical reasons, in this paper we will be forced to assume that PP is strictly positive, albeit still possibly very close to zero. This will be needed in proving the existence of strong solutions to (1.9)–(1.14) in the case of a singular potential (cf. also [8, 21] for similar assumptions).

The external sources uu and ww are the controls that we are going to use in our optimal control problem to direct the evolution of the system towards suitable targets. In the bio-medical applications, they are interpreted as external therapies acting on the tumor: uu can represent a radiotherapy (distributed through the function hh) acting on the proliferation of the tumor cells, whereas ww can be seen as a chemotherapy acting on the tumor through drugs or antiangiogenic therapy (cf., e.g., [14]).

Finally, we complement the problem with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions and given initial data:

∂𝐧φ=∂𝐧μ=∂𝐧σ=0\displaystyle\partial_{\bf n}\varphi=\partial_{\bf n}\mu=\partial_{\bf n}\sigma=0\qquad on ​(0,T)×∂Ω,\displaystyle\text{on }(0,T)\times\partial\Omega\,, (1.7)
φ⁡(0)=φ0,σ⁡(0)=σ0\displaystyle\varphi(0)=\varphi_{0}\,,\quad\sigma(0)=\sigma_{0}\qquad in ​Ω.\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega\,. (1.8)

The corresponding nonlocal problem, studied (in some cases with extra regularizing terms), e.g., in [21, 24, 25], is given by the following PDE system in (0,T)×Ω(0,T)\times\Omega

∂tφε−div(m(φε)∇με)=Rε−h(φε)uε,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\varphi_{\varepsilon}-\operatorname{div}(m(\varphi_{\varepsilon})\nabla\mu_{\varepsilon})=R_{\varepsilon}-h(\varphi_{\varepsilon})u_{\varepsilon}, (1.9)
Rε=P⁡(φε)​(σε+χ⁡(1−φε)−με),\displaystyle R_{\varepsilon}=P(\varphi_{\varepsilon})(\sigma_{\varepsilon}+\chi(1-\varphi_{\varepsilon})-\mu_{\varepsilon}), (1.10)
με=τ​∂tφε+(Jε∗1)​φε−Jε∗φε+ψ′​(φε)−χ​σε,\displaystyle\mu_{\varepsilon}=\tau\partial_{t}\varphi_{\varepsilon}+(J_{\varepsilon}*1)\varphi_{\varepsilon}-J_{\varepsilon}*\varphi_{\varepsilon}+\psi^{\prime}(\varphi_{\varepsilon})-\chi\sigma_{\varepsilon}, (1.11)
∂tσε−div[n(φε)∇(σε+χ(1−φε))]=−Rε+wε,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\sigma_{\varepsilon}-\operatorname{div}[n(\varphi_{\varepsilon})\nabla(\sigma_{\varepsilon}+\chi(1-\varphi_{\varepsilon}))]=-R_{\varepsilon}+w_{\varepsilon}, (1.12)

coupled with the following initial and boundary conditions

∂𝐧με=n⁡(φε)​∂𝐧(σε−χ​φε)=0\displaystyle\partial_{\bf n}\mu_{\varepsilon}=n(\varphi_{\varepsilon})\partial_{\bf n}(\sigma_{\varepsilon}-\chi\varphi_{\varepsilon})=0\qquad on ​(0,T)×∂Ω,\displaystyle\text{on }(0,T)\times\partial\Omega\,, (1.13)
φε​(0)=φ0,ε,σε​(0)=σ0,ε\displaystyle\varphi_{\varepsilon}(0)=\varphi_{0,\varepsilon}\,,\quad\sigma_{\varepsilon}(0)=\sigma_{0,\varepsilon}\qquad in ​Ω.\displaystyle\text{in }\Omega\,. (1.14)

The free energy associated to the local system (1.1)–(1.8) reads as

ℰ⁡(φ,σ):=∫Ω(|∇φ|22+ψ⁡(φ)+12​|σ|2+χ​σ​(1−φ))​d​x,\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\varphi,\sigma):=\int_{\Omega}\left(\frac{|\nabla\varphi|^{2}}{2}+\psi(\varphi)+\frac{1}{2}|\sigma|^{2}+\chi\sigma(1-\varphi)\right)\textrm{d}x,

where the first two terms form the well-known Modica–Mortola energy, leading to phase separation and surface tension effects.

The energetics of the nonlocal variant (1.9)–(1.14) of (1.1)–(1.8) are encoded by the following nonlocal free energy where the Dirichlet contribution in ℰ\mathcal{E} is replaced by the following nonlocal counterpart:

∫Ω∫Ω14​Jε​(x−y)​(φ⁡(x)−φ⁡(y))2​d​x​d​y,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\int_{\Omega}\frac{1}{4}J_{\varepsilon}(x-y)(\varphi(x)-\varphi(y))^{2}\textrm{d}x\,\textrm{d}y,

where JεJ_{\varepsilon} is a symmetric interaction kernel defined on Ω×Ω\Omega\times\Omega.

In many different biological models, nonlocal interactions have been used to describe competition for space and degradation [42], spatial redistribution [6, 35], and cell-to-cell adhesion [4, 9, 32] and, at least in a formal way, the nonlocal dynamics approach the local ones when the family of interaction kernels JεJ_{\varepsilon} concentrates around the origin.

Our main contribution is a rigorous characterization of such nonlocal-to-local asymptotics both for the tumor-growth model introduced above, as well as for an associated control problem, which we describe below.

(CP) Minimise the cost functional

𝒥⁡(φ,σ,u,w)=αΩ2​∫Ω|φ⁡(T)−φΩ|2+αQ2​∫0T∫Ω|φ−φQ|2+βQ2​∫0T∫Ω|σ−σQ|2+αu2∫0T∫Ω|u|2+βw2∫0T∫Ω|w|2,\begin{split}\mathcal{J}(\varphi,\sigma,u,w)&=\,\frac{\alpha_{\Omega}}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\varphi(T)-\varphi_{\Omega}|^{2}+\frac{\alpha_{Q}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|\varphi-\varphi_{Q}|^{2}+\frac{\beta_{Q}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|\sigma-\sigma_{Q}|^{2}\\ &\quad+\frac{\alpha_{u}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|u|^{2}+\frac{\beta_{w}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|w|^{2}\,,\end{split} (1.15)

subject to the control constraints

u∈𝒰a​d:={u∈L∞(QT)∩H1(0,T;L2(Ω))∣umin≤u≤umax a.e. in QT,∥u∥H1​(0,T,L2​(Ω))≤M},w∈𝒱a​d:={w∈L∞​(QT)∣wmin≤w≤wmax​ a.e. in ​QT},\begin{split}&u\in\mathcal{U}_{ad}:=\{u\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})\cap H^{1}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega))\mid u_{\text{min}}\leq u\leq u_{\text{max}}\text{ a.e. in }Q_{T},\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\|u\|_{H^{1}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega))}\leq M\},\\ &w\in\mathcal{V}_{ad}:=\{w\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})\mid w_{\text{min}}\leq w\leq w_{\text{max}}\text{ a.e. in }Q_{T}\},\end{split} (1.16)

and to the nonlocal state system (1.9)-(1.14).

The cost functional 𝒥\mathcal{J} is a standard tracking type cost functional, where the constants αΩ,αQ,βQ,αu,βw\alpha_{\Omega},\alpha_{Q},\beta_{Q},\alpha_{u},\beta_{w} are non-negative parameters that can be used to weigh the target functions φΩ\varphi_{\Omega} (a final target for the tumor distribution), φQ\varphi_{Q} (a desired tumor evolution), as well as σQ\sigma_{Q} (desired evolution for the nutrient). Finally, the last two terms in the cost functional penalise large use of radiotherapy or drugs, which could still harm vital organs of the patient. From the point of view of biological applications, the most natural choice for 𝒰a​d\mathcal{U}_{ad} would be 𝒰a​d={u∈L∞​(QT)|umin≤u≤um​a​x​a.e. in ​QT}\mathcal{U}_{ad}=\{u\in L^{\infty}(Q_{T})|u_{\rm min}\leq u\leq u_{max}\,\text{a.e. in }Q_{T}\}. The higher regularity requirement u∈H1​(0,T,L2​(Ω))u\in H^{1}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)) in (1.16) is needed in order to achieve well-posedness owing to the fact that uu acts as source term in the Cahn-Hilliard equation (see also [21, Theorems 3.5 and 3.7]).

Our main result is twofold. First, in Theorem 3.1 we show that solutions to the nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard tumor-growth systems above converge, as ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0, to solutions of its corresponding local counterpart. Second, starting from the nonlocal optimal control problem described above, in Theorems 4.1 and 5.1 we pass to the limit as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 in the associated optimality conditions and adjoint system, recently identified in [21]. As a result, in Theorem 5.2 we derive first order necessary optimality conditions for the control problem driven by the same cost functional 𝒥\mathcal{J} as in (1.15) and encoded by the local system (1.1)–(1.8) without imposing any extra regularity or differentiability assumptions on the local solution operator. Indeed, one of the main advantages of the nonlocal setting is that more regularity results are usually available and so, having at disposal rigorous nonlocal-to-local convergence results, gives us the opportunity to approximate solutions to local phase-field systems with the solutions to the corresponding nonlocal ones. For completeness we point out that from a modeling point of view, it would be meaningful to incorporate in 𝒥\mathcal{J} a further term enforcing a final target for the nutrient. Handling such mathematical term is, currently, still out of reach: In fact, in order to characterize the asymptotics of the final-time behavior of the nutrient as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 in the adjoint problem, the presence of the chemotaxis coefficient χ\chi would require stronger nonlocal-to-local convergences compared to the ones which we deduce in this contribution, cf. Section 5.

The proof of Theorem 3.1 relies on the establishment of uniform a-priori bounds for the solutions to the nonlocal system, as well as on a combination of the theory for maximal monotone graphs with some interpolation lemmas established in [18], and on a further compactness arguments for the chemotaxis, chemical-reaction term and proliferation function. Theorem 4.1 exploits essentially the variational structure of the control problems and is based on choosing the right competitors in the local and nonlocal settings. The starting point for identifying first-order optimality conditions for the local control problem in Theorems 4.1, 5.1, and 5.2 are the results in [21]. Relying on such characterizations of the optimality conditions and of the dual systems for the nonlocal case, by choosing suitable test functions for the nonlocal dual system we establish ε\varepsilon-independent uniform estimates which eventually allow us to pass to the limit and characterize the local asymptotics for the control problem.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we specify our mathematical setting and recall a few preliminary results from [21] on the well-posedness of the system for ε>0\varepsilon>0 fixed. In Section 3 we state and prove Theorem 3.1. Section 4 is entirely devoted to the local and nonlocal control problems: after specifying our working assumptions, we recall the characterization of the dual system and of the first-order optimality conditions in [21] and we state and prove Theorem 4.1. Eventually, Section 5 focuses on the passage to the limit in the nonlocal optimality conditions and on the identification of the corresponding local ones, and consists of the statements and proofs of Theorems 5.1 and 5.2.

    (φ0,ε,σ0,ε)→(φ0,σ0)in ​H×Has ​ε↘0,\displaystyle(\varphi_{0,\varepsilon},\sigma_{0,\varepsilon})\to(\varphi_{0},\sigma_{0})\quad\text{in }H\times H\qquad\text{as }\varepsilon\searrow 0\,, (2.7)
    supε∈(0,ε0)(Eε​(φ0,ε)+‖ψ⁡(φ0,ε)‖L1​(Ω)+τ​‖φ0,ε‖L6​(Ω)6)<+∞.\displaystyle\sup_{\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0})}\left(E_{\varepsilon}(\varphi_{0,\varepsilon})+\|\psi(\varphi_{0,\varepsilon})\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}+\tau\|\varphi_{0,\varepsilon}\|^{6}_{L^{6}(\Omega)}\right)<+\infty\,. (2.8)

We point out that the polynomial potentials in (1.5) fall within our analysis. In this setting, the nonlocal problem at ε>0\varepsilon>0 fixed has been widely studied in [24], also in the setting of degenerate mobilities but without viscous regularisation. In our setting, the viscosity contribution allows us to refine the assumptions and exploit the results of [21] instead. We recall here the weak existence result for the nonlocal problem proven in [21, Thm. 2.3].

Theorem 2.1 (Well-posedness: ε>0\varepsilon>0).

Assume A1–A7 and let ε∈(0,ε0)\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}). Then, for every

(u,w)∈[L∞​(Q)∩H1​(0,T,H)]×L∞​(Q),(u,w)\in[L^{\infty}(Q)\cap H^{1}(0,T;H)]\times L^{\infty}(Q)\,, (2.9)

3. Nonlocal-to-local convergence of the state systems

The first main result of this paper is the convergence of the nonlocal system (1.9)–(1.12) to the local one (1.1)–(1.4), as ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0. This shows, as a byproduct, existence of weak solutions for the local problem.

almost everywhere in (0,T)(0,T), for every ζ∈V\zeta\in V. Moreover, as ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0 there holds

−div(m(φε)∇με)⇀−div(m(φ)∇μ)\displaystyle-\operatorname{div}(m(\varphi_{\varepsilon})\nabla\mu_{\varepsilon})\rightharpoonup-\operatorname{div}(m(\varphi)\nabla\mu)\qquad in ​Lp​(0,T,W∗),\displaystyle\text{in }L^{p}(0,T;W^{*})\,,

where, by assumption A5,

|P⁡(φε)|≤M⁡(1+|φε|4).|P(\varphi_{\varepsilon})|\leq M\left(1+|\varphi_{\varepsilon}|^{4}\right)\,.

Now, (|φε|4)ε(|\varphi_{\varepsilon}|^{4})_{\varepsilon} is bounded in L∞​(0,T,L3/2​(Ω))L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{3/2}(\Omega)) by (3.21), hence the Vitali’s dominated convergence theorem yields

Letting ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0 in the weak formulation of the nonlocal system in Theorem 2.1, we pass to the limit and obtain exactly the variational formulation of the local system in Theorem 3.1, for any test function ζ∈W\zeta\in W. σε​(t)→σ⁡(t)in ​H∀t∈[0,T].\sigma_{\varepsilon}(t)\to\sigma(t)\quad\text{in }H\quad\forall\,t\in[0,T]\,.

This concludes the proof of Theorem 3.1.

4. The optimal control problem

Once the nonlocal-to-local convergence of the state-system is established, we are ready to state the optimal control problem. In this direction, we introduce the following assumptions.

  1. C1

    The space of admissible controls is defined as

    𝒰\displaystyle\mathcal{U} :={(u,w)∈[L∞(Q)∩H1(0,T;H)]×L∞(Q):\displaystyle:=\left\{(u,w)\in[L^{\infty}(Q)\cap H^{1}(0,T;H)]\times L^{\infty}(Q):\right.
    um​i​n≤u≤um​a​x,wm​i​n≤w≤wm​a​xa.e. in Q,\displaystyle\qquad\left.\;u_{min}\leq u\leq u_{max}\,,\quad w_{min}\leq w\leq w_{max}\quad\text{a.e.~in }Q\,,\right.
    ∥u∥L∞​(Q)∩H1​(0,T,H)+∥w∥L∞​(Q)≤C𝒰},\displaystyle\qquad\left.\;\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(Q)\cap H^{1}(0,T;H)}+\|w\|_{L^{\infty}(Q)}\leq C_{\mathcal{U}}\right\}\,,

    where um​i​n,um​a​x,wm​i​n,wm​a​x∈L∞​(Q)u_{min},u_{max},w_{min},w_{max}\in L^{\infty}(Q), um​i​n≥0u_{min}\geq 0 a.e. in QQ, and C𝒰>0C_{\mathcal{U}}>0 is a prescribed constant.

  2. C2

    The coefficients αΩ,αQ,βQ,αu,βw\alpha_{\Omega},\alpha_{Q},\beta_{Q},\alpha_{u},\beta_{w} are nonnegative but not all zero.

  3. C3

    The targets satisfy φΩ∈H\varphi_{\Omega}\in H and φQ,σQ∈L2​(0,T,H)\varphi_{Q},\sigma_{Q}\in L^{2}(0,T;H).

  4. C4

    The proliferation and truncation functions satisfy P,h∈C2​(ℝ)∩W1,∞​(ℝ)P,h\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R})\cap W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}).

In this setting, the optimisation problem associated to the local state-system reads:

(CP) Minimise the cost functional

𝒥⁡(φ,σ,u,w)=αΩ2​∫Ω|φ⁡(T)−φΩ|2+αQ2​∫0T∫Ω|φ−φQ|2+βQ2​∫0T∫Ω|σ−σQ|2+αu2∫0T∫Ω|u|2+βw2∫0T∫Ω|w|2,\begin{split}\mathcal{J}(\varphi,\sigma,u,w)&=\,\frac{\alpha_{\Omega}}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\varphi(T)-\varphi_{\Omega}|^{2}+\frac{\alpha_{Q}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|\varphi-\varphi_{Q}|^{2}+\frac{\beta_{Q}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|\sigma-\sigma_{Q}|^{2}\\ &\quad+\frac{\alpha_{u}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|u|^{2}+\frac{\beta_{w}}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}|w|^{2}\,,\end{split} (4.1)

subject to the control constraint (u,w)∈𝒰(u,w)\in\mathcal{U}, where (φ,μ,σ)(\varphi,\mu,\sigma) is a weak solution to the local state system associated to (u,w)(u,w) in the sense of conditions (3.1)–(3.6).

In the setting A1–A7, B1–B5, C1–C4, for every admissible control (u,w)∈𝒰(u,w)\in\mathcal{U}, the local state system admits a unique solution (φ,μ,σ)(\varphi,\mu,\sigma) in the sense of (3.1)–(3.6). Hence, the solution map

𝒮:𝒰→\displaystyle\mathcal{S}:\mathcal{U}\to [H1​(0,T,H)∩L∞​(0,T,V)∩L2​(0,T,H3​(Ω))]×[H1​(0,T,V∗)∩L2​(0,T,V)]\displaystyle[H^{1}(0,T;H)\cap L^{\infty}(0,T;V)\cap L^{2}(0,T;H^{3}(\Omega))]\times[H^{1}(0,T;V^{*})\cap L^{2}(0,T;V)]

is well-defined as

𝒮:(u,w)↦(φ,σ).\mathcal{S}:(u,w)\mapsto(\varphi,\sigma)\,.

Hence, the optimisation problem (CP) can be written in so-called reduced form and we define optimal control for problem (CP) any (u¯,w¯)∈𝒰(\overline{u},\overline{w})\in\mathcal{U} such that

𝒥⁡(𝒮⁡(u¯,w¯),u¯,w¯)=min(u,w)∈𝒰⁡𝒥⁡(𝒮⁡(u,w),u,w).\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{S}(\overline{u},\overline{w}),\overline{u},\overline{w})=\min_{(u,w)\in\mathcal{U}}\mathcal{J}(\mathcal{S}(u,w),u,w)\,.

Existence of optimal controls for (CP) follows directly by variational arguments.

Proposition 4.1 (Existence of optimal controls for (CP)).

Assume A1–A7, B1–B5, C1–C4. Then, the problem (CP) admits at least an optimal control (u¯,w¯)∈𝒰(\overline{u},\overline{w})\in\mathcal{U}.

Proof of Proposition 4.1.

This is a direct consequence of the direct method of calculus of variations. For a detailed proof in the nonlocal case we refer to [21, Thm 4.2]: this can be easily adapted to the local case with no additional technical difficulties. ∎

Remark 4.1.

Let us notice that the uniqueness of the optimal control is not to be expected here, because of the nonlinearity of the state system, which destroys the convexity of the problem.

The main issue on which we focus in this paper is the identification of first order conditions for optimality related to optimal controls for (CP). Instead of tackling the optimisation problem directly at the local level, we exploit a suitable approximation of (CP) via some optimisation problems (CP)ε involving the nonlocal system. More specifically, (CP)ε will be constructed in such a way that the optimal controls (u¯ε)ε(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon} of (CP)ε converge to a prescribed optimal control u¯\overline{u} of (CP). The necessary conditions for optimality for (CP)ε are available in the literature in terms of a suitable dual system: by proving an analogous nonlocal-to-local convergence result for such dual systems, we will then pass to the limit in the first order conditions for optimality for (CP)ε and deduce the corresponding ones for (CP). This will avoid the imposition of extra regularity on the solutions to the local problem, which would be needed should one tackle the local optimisation directly via differentiability of 𝒮\mathcal{S} for example.

4.1. The adapted optimal control problem

Let us introduce now the family (CP)ε of adapted optimal control problems: we recall that we work in the setting A1–A7, B1–B5, C1–C4.

Let (u¯,w¯)∈𝒰(\overline{u},\overline{w})\in\mathcal{U} be an optimal control for the problem (CP) and let (φ¯,σ¯):=𝒮⁡(u¯,w¯)(\overline{\varphi},\overline{\sigma}):=\mathcal{S}(\overline{u},\overline{w}) be its corresponding optimal state. For every ε∈(0,ε0)\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}), we introduce the following adapted optimisation problem.

(CP)ε Minimise the cost functional

𝒥ε​(ϕε,σε,u,w)=𝒥⁡(ϕε,σε,u,w)+12​‖u−u¯‖L2​(0,T,H)2+12​‖w−w¯‖L2​(0,T,H)2\begin{split}\mathcal{J_{\varepsilon}}(\phi_{\varepsilon},\sigma_{\varepsilon},u,w)&=\mathcal{J}(\phi_{\varepsilon},\sigma_{\varepsilon},u,w)+\frac{1}{2}\|u-\overline{u}\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H)}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|w-\overline{w}\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H)}^{2}\end{split} (4.2)

subject to the control constraint (u,w)∈𝒰(u,w)\in\mathcal{U}, where (φε,με,σε)(\varphi_{\varepsilon},\mu_{\varepsilon},\sigma_{\varepsilon}) is the unique strong solution to the nonlocal state system associated to (u,w)(u,w) in the sense of conditions (2.18)–(2.24).

Since the nonlocal state system is well posed in the sense of Theorem 2.2, the nonlocal solution map

𝒮ε:𝒰→\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\varepsilon}:\mathcal{U}\to [W1,∞​(0,T,H)∩H1​(0,T,H2​(Ω))]×[H1​(0,T,H)∩L∞​(0,T,V)∩L2​(0,T,W)]\displaystyle[W^{1,\infty}(0,T;H)\cap H^{1}(0,T;H^{2}(\Omega))]\times[H^{1}(0,T;H)\cap L^{\infty}(0,T;V)\cap L^{2}(0,T;W)]

is well-defined as

𝒮ε:(u,w)↦(φε,σε).\mathcal{S}_{\varepsilon}:(u,w)\mapsto(\varphi_{\varepsilon},\sigma_{\varepsilon})\,.

Hence, also the optimisation problem (CP)ε can be written in reduced form and we define optimal control for the problem (CP)ε any (u¯ε,w¯ε)∈𝒰(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\overline{w}_{\varepsilon})\in\mathcal{U} such that

𝒥ε​(𝒮ε​(u¯ε,w¯ε),u¯ε,w¯ε)=min(u,w)∈𝒰⁡𝒥ε​(𝒮ε​(u,w),u,w).\mathcal{J}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{S}_{\varepsilon}(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\overline{w}_{\varepsilon}),\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\overline{w}_{\varepsilon})=\min_{(u,w)\in\mathcal{U}}\mathcal{J}_{\varepsilon}(\mathcal{S}_{\varepsilon}(u,w),u,w)\,.

Note that the existence of optimal controls for (CP)ε follows by [21, Thm. 4.2]. In the theorem below we characterize the local asymptotics for optimal controls associated to (CP)ε.

4.2. First order conditions for the adapted problem

Let us focus here on the first order conditions for optimality for the adapted problem (CP)ε. Thanks to the results in [21], these can be written in terms of a variational inequality involving the solutions of a suitable adjoint, or dual, system.

In this direction, the following result ensures that the dual system is indeed well posed.

Theorem 4.2 (Well posedness of the nonlocal dual system).

Assume A1–A7, B1–B5, C1–C4, and let ε∈(0,ε0)\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}). Let (u¯ε,w¯ε)∈𝒰(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\overline{w}_{\varepsilon})\in\mathcal{U} and let (φ¯ε,σ¯ε):=𝒮ε​(u¯,w¯)(\overline{\varphi}_{\varepsilon},\overline{\sigma}_{\varepsilon}):=\mathcal{S}_{\varepsilon}(\overline{u},\overline{w}) be the solution to the nonlocal state system. Then, there exists a unique triplet (pε,qε,rε)(p_{\varepsilon},q_{\varepsilon},r_{\varepsilon}), with

pε∈L2​(0,T,W),\displaystyle p_{\varepsilon}\in L^{2}(0,T;W)\,, (4.4)
qε∈L2​(0,T,H),\displaystyle q_{\varepsilon}\in L^{2}(0,T;H)\,, (4.5)
rε∈H1​(0,T,H)∩L∞​(0,T,V)∩L2​(0,T,W),\displaystyle r_{\varepsilon}\in H^{1}(0,T;H)\cap L^{\infty}(0,T;V)\cap L^{2}(0,T;W)\,, (4.6)
pε+τ​qε∈H1​(0,T,H),\displaystyle p_{\varepsilon}+\tau q_{\varepsilon}\in H^{1}(0,T;H)\,, (4.7)

such that

(pε+τ​qε)​(T)=αΩ​(φ¯ε​(T)−φΩ),rε​(T)=0,(p_{\varepsilon}+\tau q_{\varepsilon})(T)=\alpha_{\Omega}(\overline{\varphi}_{\varepsilon}(T)-\varphi_{\Omega})\,,\qquad r_{\varepsilon}(T)=0\,, (4.8)

and

The well posedness of the adjoint system allows then to formulate first order conditions for optimality for the adapted problem (CP)ε. In this sense, we have the following result.

Theorem 4.3 (First order conditions for (CP)ε).

Assume A1–A7, B1–B5, C1–C4, let ε∈(0,ε0)\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0}), let (u¯,w¯)∈𝒰(\overline{u},\overline{w})\in\mathcal{U} be an optimal control for (CP), let (u¯ε,w¯ε)∈𝒰(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\overline{w}_{\varepsilon})\in\mathcal{U} be an optimal control for (CP)ε, and let (φ¯ε,σ¯ε):=𝒮ε​(u¯ε,w¯ε)(\overline{\varphi}_{\varepsilon},\overline{\sigma}_{\varepsilon}):=\mathcal{S}_{\varepsilon}(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\overline{w}_{\varepsilon}) be the respective optimal state of the nonlocal system. Then, if (pε,qε,rε)(p_{\varepsilon},q_{\varepsilon},r_{\varepsilon}) is the unique solution to the nonlocal dual system in the sense of (4.4)–(4.11), it holds for every (u,w)∈𝒰(u,w)\in\mathcal{U} that

∫Q(−h⁡(φ¯ε)​pε+αu​u¯ε+u¯ε−u¯)​(u−u¯ε)​d​x​d​s+∫Q(rε+βw​w¯ε+w¯ε−w¯)​(w−w¯ε)​d​x​d​s≥0.\int_{Q}(-h(\overline{\varphi}_{\varepsilon})p_{\varepsilon}+\alpha_{u}\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}+\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}-\overline{u})(u-\overline{u}_{\varepsilon})\,\textrm{d}x\textrm{d}s+\int_{Q}(r_{\varepsilon}+\beta_{w}\overline{w}_{\varepsilon}+\overline{w}_{\varepsilon}-\overline{w})(w-\overline{w}_{\varepsilon})\,\textrm{d}x\textrm{d}s\geq 0\,. (4.12)
Proof of Theorem 4.3.

This follows directly from [21, Thm. 4.8]. ∎

5. Nonlocal-to-local convergence of the optimal control problems

This section is devoted to proving first order conditions for optimality for the limit problem (CP), by passing to the limit as ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0 in the first order conditions for (CP)ε. This requires two passages to the limit, one in the dual system obtained in Theorem 4.2 and one in the variational inequality of Theorem 4.1. The two main results that we prove are the following.

Theorem 5.1 (Convergence of the dual systems).

Assume A1–A7, B1–B5, C1–C4, let {(u¯ε,w¯ε)}ε∈(0,ε0)⊂𝒰\{(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\overline{w}_{\varepsilon})\}_{\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0})}\subset\mathcal{U} be a family of admissible controls, let {(φ¯ε,σ¯ε):=𝒮ε(u¯ε,w¯ε)}ε∈(0,ε0)\{(\overline{\varphi}_{\varepsilon},\overline{\sigma}_{\varepsilon}):=\mathcal{S}_{\varepsilon}(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\overline{w}_{\varepsilon})\}_{\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0})} be the corresponding family of nonlocal states, and let {(pε,qε,rε)}ε∈(0,ε0)\{(p_{\varepsilon},q_{\varepsilon},r_{\varepsilon})\}_{\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_{0})} be the corresponding solutions to the nonlocal dual problem in the sense of (4.4)–(4.11). Let also (u¯,w¯)∈𝒰(\overline{u},\overline{w})\in\mathcal{U} be an admissible control such that, as ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0,

u¯ε⇀∗u¯\displaystyle\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle*}}{{\rightharpoonup}}\overline{u}\quad in ​L∞​(Q)∩H1​(0,T,H),\displaystyle\text{in }L^{\infty}(Q)\cap H^{1}(0,T;H)\,,
w¯ε⇀∗w¯\displaystyle\overline{w}_{\varepsilon}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle*}}{{\rightharpoonup}}\overline{w}\quad in ​L∞​(Q),\displaystyle\text{in }L^{\infty}(Q)\,,

and let (φ¯,σ¯):=𝒮⁡(u¯,w¯)(\overline{\varphi},\overline{\sigma}):=\mathcal{S}(\overline{u},\overline{w}) be the corresponding local state. Then, there exists a unique triplet (p,q,r)(p,q,r), with

p∈L2​(0,T,W),\displaystyle p\in L^{2}(0,T;W)\,, (5.1)
q∈L2​(0,T,V),\displaystyle q\in L^{2}(0,T;V)\,, (5.2)
r∈H1​(0,T,H)∩L∞​(0,T,V)∩L2​(0,T,W),\displaystyle r\in H^{1}(0,T;H)\cap L^{\infty}(0,T;V)\cap L^{2}(0,T;W)\,, (5.3)
p+τ​q∈H1​(0,T,V∗)∩L∞​(0,T,H),\displaystyle p+\tau q\in H^{1}(0,T;V^{*})\cap L^{\infty}(0,T;H)\,, (5.4)

such that

(p+τ​q)​(T)=αΩ​(φ¯​(T)−φΩ),r⁡(T)=0,(p+\tau q)(T)=\alpha_{\Omega}(\overline{\varphi}(T)-\varphi_{\Omega})\,,\qquad r(T)=0\,, (5.5)

and

=P′​(φ¯)​(σ¯+χ⁡(1−φ¯)−μ¯)​(p−r)−h′​(φ¯)​u¯​p+αQ​(φ¯−φQ),\displaystyle\qquad=P^{\prime}(\overline{\varphi})(\overline{\sigma}+\chi(1-\overline{\varphi})-\overline{\mu})(p-r)-h^{\prime}(\overline{\varphi})\overline{u}p+\alpha_{Q}(\overline{\varphi}-\varphi_{Q})\,, (5.6)

qε→q\displaystyle q_{\varepsilon}\to q\quad in ​L2​(0,T,H),\displaystyle\text{in }L^{2}(0,T;H)\,, (5.11)

Assume A1–A7, B1–B5, C1–C4, let (u¯,w¯)∈𝒰(\overline{u},\overline{w})\in\mathcal{U} be an optimal control for (CP), and let (φ¯,σ¯):=𝒮⁡(u¯,w¯)(\overline{\varphi},\overline{\sigma}):=\mathcal{S}(\overline{u},\overline{w}) be the respective optimal state of the local system. Then, if (p,q,r)(p,q,r) is the unique solution to the local dual system in the sense of (5.1)–(5.8), for every (u,w)∈𝒰(u,w)\in\mathcal{U} there holds

∫Q(−h⁡(φ¯)​p+αu​u¯)​(u−u¯)​d​x​d​s+∫Q(r+βw​w¯)​(w−w¯)​d​x​d​s≥0.\int_{Q}(-h(\overline{\varphi})p+\alpha_{u}\overline{u})(u-\overline{u})\,\textrm{d}x\textrm{d}s+\int_{Q}(r+\beta_{w}\overline{w})(w-\overline{w})\,\textrm{d}x\textrm{d}s\geq 0\,. (5.16)

‖pε‖L2​(0,T,V)≤M,\displaystyle\|p_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(0,T;V)}\leq M\,, (5.24)

‖qε‖L2​(0,T,H)+‖Eε​(qε)‖L1​(0,T)≤M,\displaystyle\|q_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H)}+\|E_{\varepsilon}(q_{\varepsilon})\|_{L^{1}(0,T)}\leq M\,, (5.26)
‖rε‖H1​(0,T,H)∩L∞​(0,T,V)≤M,\displaystyle\|r_{\varepsilon}\|_{H^{1}(0,T;H)\cap L^{\infty}(0,T;V)}\leq M\,, (5.27)

where the constant MM is independent of ε\varepsilon. In particular, (5.25), the boundedness of (φ¯ε)ε(\overline{\varphi}_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon} in L∞​(0,T,L6​(Ω))L^{\infty}(0,T;L^{6}(\Omega)), and the inclusion L6/5​(Ω)↪V∗L^{6/5}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow V^{*} imply that

‖Bε​(qε)‖L2​(0,T,V∗)+‖ψ′′​(φ¯ε)​qε‖L2​(0,T,V∗)≤M.\|B_{\varepsilon}(q_{\varepsilon})\|_{L^{2}(0,T;V^{*})}+\|\psi^{\prime\prime}(\overline{\varphi}_{\varepsilon})q_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(0,T;V^{*})}\leq M\,. (5.28)

Hence a direct comparison in (4.9)–(4.11) yields also

‖pε‖L2​(0,T,W)≤M,\displaystyle\|p_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(0,T;W)}\leq M\,, (5.29)
‖pε+τ​qε‖H1​(0,T,V∗)≤M,\displaystyle\|p_{\varepsilon}+\tau q_{\varepsilon}\|_{H^{1}(0,T;V^{*})}\leq M\,, (5.30)
‖rε‖L2​(0,T,W)≤M.\displaystyle\|r_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{2}(0,T;W)}\leq M\,. (5.31)

5.2. Passage to the limit in the dual system

The estimates (5.24)–(5.31) imply the existence of a triplet (p,q,r)(p,q,r) satisfying (5.1)–(5.5), as well as, as ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0 along a subsequence, the convergences (5.9)–(5.10) and (5.12)–(5.15). As for (5.11), we note that by comparison one obtains first that qε→qq_{\varepsilon}\to q in L2​(0,T,V∗)L^{2}(0,T;V^{*}), and this implies also qε→qq_{\varepsilon}\to q in L2​(0,T,H)L^{2}(0,T;H) by the compactness lemma [18, Lem. 3.4]. Moreover, from the strong convergence (5.11) and the estimate (5.29), thanks to [18, Prop. 3.1] (in a suitable integrated-in-time formulation) we deduce that q∈L2​(0,T,V)q\in L^{2}(0,T;V) and that

Bε​(qε)⇀B⁡(q)in ​L2​(0,T,V∗).B_{\varepsilon}(q_{\varepsilon})\rightharpoonup B(q)\quad\text{in }L^{2}(0,T;V^{*})\,.

Since P′P^{\prime} and h′h^{\prime} are bounded and continuous, it is immediate to check that all the terms in (4.9)–(4.11) pass to the limit as ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0, and (5.6)–(5.8) follow. This concludes the proof of existence and convergence in Theorem 5.1. We are only left with showing that the solution to the local dual system is unique: to this end, it is enough to prove that if (p,q,r)(p,q,r) is a solution to the homogeneous problem, i.e. (5.1)–(5.8) with formally αΩ=αQ=βQ=0\alpha_{\Omega}=\alpha_{Q}=\beta_{Q}=0, then p=q=r=0p=q=r=0. Now, it is straightforward to check that the same estimate performed on the nonlocal dual system in Subsection 5.1 can be repeated in this context with elementary adaptations: this yields

‖p⁡(t)+τ​q​(t)‖H2+‖r⁡(t)‖V2+∫tT(‖q‖H2+‖∇q‖H2+‖p‖V2+‖∂tr‖H2+‖r‖V2)​d​s\displaystyle\|p(t)+\tau q(t)\|_{H}^{2}+\|r(t)\|^{2}_{V}+\int_{t}^{T}\left(\|q\|_{H}^{2}+\|\nabla q\|_{H}^{2}+\|p\|_{V}^{2}+\|\partial_{t}r\|_{H}^{2}+\|r\|_{V}^{2}\right)\,\textrm{d}s
≤C~​(∫tT‖r‖H2​d​s+∫tT(1+‖σ¯+χ⁡(1−φ¯)‖V2+‖μ¯‖V2)​‖p+τ​q‖H2​d​s),\displaystyle\leq\tilde{C}\left(\int_{t}^{T}\|r\|_{H}^{2}\,\textrm{d}s+\int_{t}^{T}\left(1+\|\overline{\sigma}+\chi(1-\overline{\varphi})\|_{V}^{2}+\|\overline{\mu}\|_{V}^{2}\right)\|p+\tau q\|_{H}^{2}\,\textrm{d}s\right)\,,

so that the Gronwall lemma implies that p=q=r=0p=q=r=0. This concludes the proof of Theorem 5.1.

5.3. Passage to the limit in the first order conditions

We are ready to prove now Theorem 5.2. Given an optimal control (u¯,w¯)(\overline{u},\overline{w}) for (CP), by Theorem 4.1 there is a sequence of optimal controls (u¯ε,w¯ε)ε(\overline{u}_{\varepsilon},\overline{w}_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon} satisfying the convergences in Theorem 4.1. Moreover, denoting by (pε,qε,rε)ε(p_{\varepsilon},q_{\varepsilon},r_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon} the solutions of the corresponding nonlocal dual systems, one has the convergences (5.9)–(5.15) by Theorem 5.1, as well as the first order conditions for optimality for (CP)ε in (4.12). Since u¯ε→u¯\overline{u}_{\varepsilon}\to\overline{u} and w¯ε→w¯\overline{w}_{\varepsilon}\to\overline{w} in L2​(0,T,H)L^{2}(0,T;H), by letting ε↘0\varepsilon\searrow 0 in (4.12) one readily obtains (5.16) by the dominated convergence theorem. This concludes the proof of Theorem 5.2.
